meta.description: Sample conversation: a 30-minute launch readiness review at Pellwood, a fictional software company. Nine invented people.

note.title: Enterprise launch review: SSO gates the date

transcript.text: Okay, launch readiness review for Pellwood Enterprise. The launch date on the plan is still Tuesday the 3rd.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: By the end of this, either we confirm the launch date, or we know the one thing that would move the date.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: The launch checklist is at nineteen of twenty-three. The four open launch items are all on today's agenda.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: And the launch page copy is done, pending the final launch date.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: Theo, short version from engineering first, then we go topic by topic.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Sure. Most of the launch scope is done.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Billing, the activity log, the new admin console. All merged, all on staging since Friday.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Load testing came back green on Sunday. Four times the beta traffic, and staging held up fine.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: So the launch scope itself is in good shape for the 3rd.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: There's one item that worries me, and I'll get to it in a minute.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Is Tuesday the 3rd the date I should plan around?
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: For now, yes. We lock it on Friday.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: We lock the launch date right after this review and the board meeting.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: And the launch date really matters on my side. Three signed customers have kickoffs booked the week of the 3rd.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: If the launch slips, I'm the one calling them. One of those kickoffs is Corbel.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Understood. Grace, Lena, raise anything that hangs on the exact launch date.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Only the help articles. They go live with the launch, and I'd like a day of buffer before the launch date.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Same here. Everything on my side hangs on the launch date, so the earlier we lock it, the better.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: My whole launch calendar says the 3rd. Moving the date costs me a few awkward emails, but it's doable.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: Okay. Theo, go ahead. The item that worries you.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Right. The real blocker is SSO. SAML login, specifically.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: SAML login works with two of our three identity providers. SSO on the third provider fails.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: It fails on signed assertions. The identity provider sends a perfectly valid response, we reject it, and the user lands back on the login page.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: And that third identity provider is the one most of the big prospects use.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Walk us through the SSO failure. Ines, you found it.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Yeah. The SAML failure is clock skew, mostly.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: Their SAML assertions arrive a few seconds early, and our SAML library rejects anything early.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: So an assertion stamped three seconds in the future counts as invalid, and the SSO login fails.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: We can loosen that. The SSO fix itself is small. Testing it against every identity provider is the slow part.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Each identity provider wants its own test tenant, and the third one took us nine days to set up.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Nine days just to get a test tenant. That identity provider is not exactly in a hurry.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: The SSO fix is on a branch already. Twelve lines, plus a setting for the SAML clock tolerance.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: And the SAML library added the same clock tolerance setting last month, so we're not inventing anything.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: Um, the SSO setup screen in the admin console is ready, by the way. Admins upload the SAML metadata file and test the connection.
transcript.speaker: speaker_8

transcript.text: Nice. Thanks, Jun.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: If the SAML test fails, the setup screen shows the raw SAML error, though. Admins will hate that.
transcript.speaker: speaker_8

transcript.text: Just so everyone hears it, I won't sign off on SSO until the signed assertion fix has been through a security review.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Totally fair.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Loosening clock tolerance on SAML is exactly the kind of change that opens a replay window.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: So two minutes of SAML clock tolerance, max, logged, and an alert on any skew above thirty seconds.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Two minutes is fine. Most of the clock skew we saw was under ten seconds.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: One test tenant drifted forty seconds, but that was a misconfigured clock on their side, not ours.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: I also want every SSO login in the activity log, successes and failures, with the identity provider.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Fair. Logging SSO login events is an hour of work.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Ines and I can pair on the SSO fix tomorrow, so the SSO review starts early.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: So the SSO fix lands by Thursday the 29th, if nothing else catches fire.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Then Ruth needs two days for the SSO review.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Two working days for the SSO review. So Monday the 2nd, at the earliest.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: That's one day of slack. Zero, really.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Yeah. It's tight.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: And SCIM provisioning is out of scope. SSO login only, accounts still get created by hand.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Right. SCIM can wait for next quarter.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Corbel won't care about SCIM. Corbel cares about SSO login on day one.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Another dependency. The SOC 2 audit.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: The SOC 2 audit window closes on the 31st, and SSO is in scope for the audit.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: The SOC 2 readiness check flagged two audit gaps. Both are closed now, with evidence.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: The SOC 2 audit covers May through October. Six months of evidence, and most of it is in good shape.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Do we have a date from the auditors yet?
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: I don't know yet.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Kestrel still hasn't confirmed the SOC 2 audit fieldwork dates.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: They said this week. I've asked twice.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: And the SOC 2 report won't exist until December. Kestrel writes the audit report after the window closes.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Can we mention SOC 2 in the announcement?
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: Hmm.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: December is way too late for the SOC 2 report. Every security questionnaire asks for it.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Corbel's procurement team asked for the SOC 2 report last Thursday. Arden asked on Monday.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Right, but there's a bridge letter. The audit firm can issue a bridge letter that covers the gap until the SOC 2 report lands.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: So the bridge letter has to cover us until the SOC 2 report lands.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: For most buyers, it will.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Corbel's security team accepted a bridge letter from their last vendor. Arden, I honestly can't say.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Arden's security team is stricter than Corbel's, for the record.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: But Kestrel only issues the bridge letter once the audit fieldwork starts.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: So the SOC 2 report and the bridge letter both wait on the audit firm.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Pretty much. The audit firm is the bottleneck for the whole SOC 2 timeline.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: If the audit slips into November, the bridge letter slips with it.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Okay. So we need the auditors on site before the 3rd.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Ideally the week before. I'll chase Kestrel on the fieldwork dates again today.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: So does any of this move the launch date?
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Honestly, I'd push it a week.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: A week. Theo, three customers have kickoffs that week.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: And I'd rather move a kickoff than launch something half-broken.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: It's not half-broken. It's one edge case for one group of customers.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: An edge case your biggest customers live in, Marcus.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Then we fix the edge case. We don't move the launch for it.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Okay, okay. Hold on.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Honestly, a calm launch beats a fast launch.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Nobody is deciding the launch date in the next two minutes.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Let's get the full picture first, and come back to the launch date at the end.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Fine.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Fine by me.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Okay. Discounts, list pricing, seat minimums, and the enterprise tier.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Pricing first, then discounts.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: The enterprise list price is forty-eight dollars a seat per month, fifty seat minimum, billed annually.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: And the list price is working. Nobody has pushed back on forty-eight, and the new pricing page converts better than the old one.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: The two big incumbents charge sixty-five and seventy a seat, so the enterprise pricing is an easy conversation.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: The pricing isn't the problem. Discounts are.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: I have three enterprise deals asking for a forty percent discount.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Forty percent is not a discount. That's a different price.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: It's a different price for logos we need on the website.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: We agreed the enterprise discount cap was twenty-five percent. In September. All of us.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: We agreed that cap before Greywater asked for three hundred seats.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Three hundred seats at list price is a hundred and seventy thousand a year. Even with forty percent off, it's the biggest deal we've ever signed.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: And it sets the pricing for every finance team that hears about it. Discounts leak, Marcus.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Sorry, are these discounts on the seat price or on the whole contract?
transcript.speaker: speaker_8

transcript.text: On the seat price only.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: The platform fee always stays at list price. Eight thousand a year, flat.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Okay, let's make the discount concrete. What's the floor on the discount?
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Twenty-five percent standard, thirty with a two-year term.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Anything deeper comes to you and finance, deal by deal.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: I can live with that discount floor. Thirty with a two-year term, and nothing deeper without a signed case study.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: A case study I can get. Greywater already offered one.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Then Greywater gets thirty percent and a two-year term, and the rest of the discount waits for the case study.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: And Arden offered a three-year term in exchange for the discount. That one I actually like.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: A three-year term changes the discount math. Bring me the Arden numbers before you agree to anything.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Deal. I'll put the discount floor in the pricing doc today.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: One more pricing thing. Halden wants monthly pricing instead of annual billing, and the pricing doc doesn't allow it.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Good. Annual billing stays in the pricing. Monthly billing lost us money on the old pricing model.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: For reference, the median discount across the beta conversions was eighteen percent.
transcript.speaker: speaker_9

transcript.text: Eighteen percent. Good, that helps the pricing story.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: How many of the enterprise deals in the pipeline need SSO?
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Six of the nine.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Corbel and Arden both made it a hard requirement in the contract. The other four deals would take it in December.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Okay, back to SSO and that third identity provider, then.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Can we ship SSO behind a flag?
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Yes, with a per-workspace flag.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: We turn SSO on for those six accounts and leave the flag off for everyone else.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: I'm fine with an SSO flag, as long as the security review still happens before any of the six switch it on.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Agreed. The SSO flag doesn't skip the security review.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: And the flag gives us an off switch. If the third identity provider still misbehaves, we flip that account back to passwords.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: Good. That takes some pressure off.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Okay, data migration risk.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Right. The data migration is the big one for me.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: The data migration moves every existing workspace onto the new permissions model.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: We ran the data migration twice on a copy of production. 1,140 workspaces, three hours and twenty minutes end to end.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: Four workspaces failed the data migration twice, all on orphaned records.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: The orphaned records come from the old sharing feature. We delete them before the data migration, with a backup.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: Those four we can fix by hand before the data migration starts.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: What's the rollback if the migration fails halfway?
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Every workspace gets its own snapshot.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: The snapshot is taken right before that workspace migrates, and restoring one workspace takes about four minutes.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: And we migrate fifty at a time, so a failure stops fifty, not the whole data migration.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: How long does the full migration take on production?
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: We've never run the data migration on the three biggest data sets, ten times the size of the copy.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: That's the real risk with the migration. The data volume, not the code.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Greywater alone has four million ledger rows. The copy we tested the migration on had nothing close.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: I can run the three biggest data sets on a separate copy this week, and have real migration numbers by Thursday.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: Do that. And if the migration runs long, it happens on Saturday, with the old model still readable.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Makes sense. We'd start the migration Saturday morning and keep the old permissions model readable during the migration.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: Each workspace goes read-only for about ten minutes while it migrates, with a migration banner instead of an error.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: And we watch the migration on a dashboard. Error rate, batch time, data copied.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: The migration dashboard pages me if the error rate passes one percent.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Every workspace owner gets an email about the migration window, with the read-only times.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: And keep the migration snapshots for thirty days after. Auditors will ask.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Thirty days of snapshots is fine. Snapshot storage is cheap compared to a failed migration.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: The permissions migration is the only step with no undo button, apart from the snapshots.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: Okay, support staffing and the support queue.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Right. Support staffing is my biggest worry. We have four support agents, and two are out that week.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: One support agent is on parental leave, and one is at her sister's wedding.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: So two support agents cover the enterprise queue and the regular queue, in the busiest support week of the year.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Last launch, support tickets tripled in the first two days, and the support queue never really recovered that week.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Who's on call for support escalations that week?
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Ines and me as primary.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Ruth backs us up on support escalations, in shifts.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: That covers engineering. I still need people on the support queue in the evenings.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Can engineering cover the evening support queue that week?
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Hmm.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Let's take the evening support queue offline. Grace, send me the gaps in the support schedule.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Will do. And I want support macros written before the 3rd, for the support agents.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: I'll pull the support tickets from the last launch, so the support macros match real tickets.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Last launch the support agents answered setup questions with screenshots. This time every support macro links to the setup guide.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: And the support queue gets a priority lane for the six SSO accounts.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Good. A priority lane in the support queue makes sense.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: I'd also like an engineer in the support channel the first morning, to unblock the support agents fast.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: That one's easy. Theo, put an engineer in the support channel, for the support queue.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Done. Ines covers the first support morning, I cover the afternoon.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: And the support agents get a half-day of SSO training on Thursday, so the support queue isn't learning live.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Beta feedback and the import bug.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: The beta feedback is mostly good, apart from the import bug. Large CSV files time out, and the import screen just says something went wrong.
transcript.speaker: speaker_8

transcript.text: How many beta accounts hit the import bug?
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Fourteen of the 212 beta accounts.
transcript.speaker: speaker_9

transcript.text: Eleven of those were importing CSV files over 50,000 rows. The other three had a byte order mark in the CSV file.
transcript.speaker: speaker_9

transcript.text: And the import bug isn't really a timeout. The importer drops the last chunk of any CSV file bigger than one upload chunk.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: So the import says it failed, but most rows actually landed. Partial imports that look complete.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: Did any of those beta accounts lose data for good?
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: No idea, honestly.
transcript.speaker: speaker_9

transcript.text: I only have the import error logs, not the customer data.
transcript.speaker: speaker_9

transcript.text: I can check. We keep the raw CSV uploads, so we can replay all fourteen imports.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: The import fix merged, and the fixed importer is in release candidate three.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: And we added a test with a sixty thousand row CSV file, so the import bug can't come back quietly.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Good. Replay the fourteen imports this week, and the import error needs a clearer message.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Agreed. I'll have new copy for the import error message tomorrow.
transcript.speaker: speaker_8

transcript.text: Send the new copy to me too. Half of those fourteen customers opened tickets about the import bug.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Halden Freight hit the import bug three times in one week. They're the loudest of the fourteen.
transcript.speaker: speaker_7

transcript.text: Halden opened four support tickets about the import bug. The last import ticket was not friendly.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Then Halden gets a personal email about the import fix, from me, today.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: And the import progress bar will show rows imported, so a partial import is visible.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: The announcement, then, and the news embargo.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Right. For the announcement, I'd move the news embargo to Wednesday.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: The analyst briefing is on Tuesday, so the news should land after the briefing, on Wednesday.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: So the news embargo lifts at nine on Wednesday the 4th. Customers get access on the 3rd, and the announcement goes out on the 4th.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: So customers get a quiet day before the news hits. I like that, actually.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Exactly. And the news story has real quotes in it.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: Two trade outlets have the story under the news embargo already.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: Good. Keep those trade outlets close.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Legal approved two of the quotes for the news story.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: The blog post and the customer email are ready. The news release is with legal until Thursday.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: And the news embargo means the trade outlets can't publish before nine on Wednesday.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: And the news embargo gives sales a morning to call the kickoff customers first.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Please keep SOC 2 out of the news release for now.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: Already done. Nothing about the audit in the news release until it's real.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: And thank you for Wednesday. That gives us a day to breathe before the news.
transcript.speaker: speaker_5

transcript.text: Okay, back to the launch date, then. Here's my proposal.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: We hold the launch date. Tuesday the 3rd.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: If the SSO piece slips past Monday, the launch date moves a week, and we say so on Monday, not on launch morning.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: I can commit to that.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: Theo, the Monday check is yours. Fix merged, review signed, or the launch date moves.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Understood. Monday at ten, before standup.
transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.text: I can live with that. I'll warn the three kickoff customers today that the launch date could move.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: And I'll tell Corbel the 3rd is likely, not promised.
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

transcript.text: Works for me.
transcript.speaker: speaker_6

transcript.text: I'll hold both launch dates in the calendar until Monday.
transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.text: Great. The launch date holds at the 3rd, with a hard check on Monday. Thanks, everyone.
transcript.speaker: speaker_1

transcript.text: Wait, one more. Are we still doing the launch webinar on the 5th?
transcript.speaker: speaker_4

note.enhanced_content:
The team reviewed launch readiness for Pellwood Enterprise and kept Tuesday the 3rd as the launch date, on condition that the SSO fix and its security review are finished by Monday the 2nd.

## Threads
- **Launch date vs. SSO.** SAML login fails on one of three identity providers, the one most large prospects use, because signed assertions arrive with clock skew. The fix is small; testing it and Ruth's review make Monday the 2nd the earliest sign-off, which leaves one day of slack. Six of the nine enterprise deals need SSO on day one.
- **SOC 2 timing.** SSO is in scope for the audit, the report will not exist until December, and Kestrel has not confirmed fieldwork dates. A bridge letter would cover most buyers, but only once fieldwork starts.
- **Enterprise pricing.** The list price ($48 a seat a month, 50-seat minimum) is holding. The pressure is on discounts: three deals are asking for 40% off, Greywater among them at 300 seats.
- **Migration and beta risk.** The permissions migration took 3h20m on a copy of production (4 of 1,140 workspaces failed) but has never run against the three largest workspaces. The CSV import bug hit 14 of 212 beta accounts; whether any data was lost is still unknown.

## Decisions Made
- Hold Tuesday the 3rd, with a hard check on Monday the 2nd. If the SSO fix or its review is not done, the launch moves a week and the team hears on Monday.
- Ship SSO behind a per-workspace flag, switched on for the six accounts only after the security review.
- Discount floor: 25% standard, 30% with a two-year term. Anything deeper needs Maya, finance and a signed case study.
- Announce on Wednesday the 4th, the day after the analyst briefing, and keep SOC 2 out of the news release until the bridge letter exists.

## Action Items
- [ ] Theo: signed-assertion fix by Thursday the 29th, with clock tolerance capped at two minutes and logged.
- [ ] Ruth: security review of the fix; chase Kestrel for fieldwork dates.
- [ ] Ines: run the migration on the three largest workspaces and report timings by Thursday; replay the 14 failed imports.
- [ ] Marcus: add the discount floor to the pricing doc; warn the three kickoff customers that the date could move.
- [ ] Grace: send Maya the gaps in the evening support schedule.
- [ ] Jun: new copy for the import error message.

## Follow-ups
- Who covers the evening support queue that week.
- Whether the launch webinar on the 5th still goes ahead.
note.enhancement_prompt: Transform the provided content into clean, well-structured notes in markdown. Preserve the user's intent and all substantive information. Remove filler, small talk, false starts, and redundant content. For personal notes, improve grammar and structure for readability. For meeting transcripts, extract key discussion points, decisions, action items, and follow-ups.
